question: According to the discussion on the triangle inequality for integrals, if for all \(n\ge m\) we have \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in[a,b]\), what inequality can we deduce for \(\displaystyle\int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx\), and why does the bound \(\varepsilon\) appear in this inequality?

The bound \(\varepsilon\) appears because the integrand \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\) is uniformly bounded by \(\varepsilon\) on the entire interval, so the integral is at most \(\varepsilon\) times the length of the interval.

question: From the definition of uniform absolute‑convergence, explain why the existence of a single \(m\) that works for all \(x\) in the domain is crucial, and how this contrasts with the pointwise convergence condition that would allow \(m\) to depend on \(x\).
answer: Uniform absolute‑convergence requires that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an \(m\) such that for all \(n\ge m\) and for all \(x\) in the domain, \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\). This single \(m\) works uniformly over the whole domain, guaranteeing that the convergence does not depend on the particular point \(x\). In contrast, pointwise convergence would allow a different \(m_x\) for each \(x\), so the bound might fail to hold uniformly across the domain.

question: Combining the uniform bound \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x\) with the triangle inequality for integrals, explain why the sequence of integrals \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx\) converges to \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\), and what role the absolute value plays in this argument.
answer: Because \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) uniformly, we have \(\displaystyle\int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx < \varepsilon(b-a)\). By the triangle inequality for integrals, \(\displaystyle\bigl|\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx - \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\bigr| \le \int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx\). Thus \(\bigl|\int_a^b f_n - \int_a^b f\bigr| < \varepsilon(b-a)\). Since \(\varepsilon\) can be made arbitrarily small, the integrals converge. The absolute value is essential to bound the difference of integrals by the integral of the absolute difference.

question: Suppose \((f_n)\) is a sequence of continuous functions on \([a,b]\) that converges uniformly to \(f\). Additionally, the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(f_{n+1}-f_n)\) converges uniformly absolutely. Using the uniform limit theorem and the definition of uniform absolute convergence, explain why \(\displaystyle \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx\).
answer: Uniform absolute convergence of the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(f_{n+1}-f_n)\) implies that the sequence of partial sums \(S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}(f_{n+1}-f_n)=f_{N+1}(x)-f_1(x)\) converges uniformly to a continuous function \(S(x)=f(x)-f_1(x)\). Hence \(f_N\) converges uniformly to \(f\). By the uniform limit theorem, \(f\) is continuous. For each \(N\), \(\int_a^b f_N(x)\,dx\) exists because \(f_N\) is continuous. Uniform convergence allows us to interchange limit and integral: \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\int_a^b f_N(x)\,dx = \int_a^b \lim_{N\to\infty} f_N(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\) Thus the equality holds.

question: It was discussed that if \(f_n\) are continuously differentiable, \(f_n \to f\) uniformly, and \(f_n'\to g\) uniformly, then \(f\) is differentiable with \(f'=g\). Using the uniform limit theorem, explain the reasoning that leads from the uniform convergence of the derivatives to the conclusion that \(f'=g\), and why uniform convergence of the derivatives is necessary for this result.
answer: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, \(f_n(x)-f_n(a)=\int_a^x f_n'(t)\,dt\). Taking limits and using the uniform limit theorem on the integrals of \(f_n'\) (which converge uniformly to \(g\)) gives \(f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt\). Differentiating both sides shows \(f'(x)=g(x)\). Uniform convergence of the derivatives is necessary to apply the uniform limit theorem to the integrals; without it, the limit of the integrals may not equal the integral of the limit.

question: In the lecture it was shown that if \(f_n\) converges uniformly to a function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) and each \(f_n\) is continuous, then \(f\) is continuous. Using this fact together with the definition of a Riemann sum, explain why the limit of the Riemann sums of \(f_n\) as the mesh of the partition tends to zero equals \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
answer: Because \(f_n \to f\) uniformly, for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\) and \(n\ge N\). For a partition \(P\) with mesh \(\|P\|\) small enough, the difference between the Riemann sums satisfies \(|S(f_n,P)-S(f,P)|\le (b-a)\cdot\varepsilon/(b-a)=\varepsilon\). Taking the limit as \(\|P\|\to0\) gives \(\lim_{\|P\|\to0}S(f_n,P)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). Thus the limit of the Riemann sums of \(f_n\) equals the integral of \(f\).

question: Consider a sequence \((f_n)\) of continuous functions on a set \(X\) that converges uniformly to a function \(f\). Using the definition of uniform absolute‑convergence given in the lecture, explain why \(f\) must be continuous, and discuss what could happen if the convergence were only pointwise.
answer: Uniform absolute‑convergence means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that for all \(n\ge N\) and all \(x\in X\) we have \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\). Because each \(f_n\) is continuous, for any fixed \(x_0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) we can find \(\delta>0\) with \(|x-x_0|<\delta\) implying \(|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|<\varepsilon\). Combining these two facts gives \(|f(x)-f(x_0)|<2\varepsilon\) for all \(x\) sufficiently close to \(x_0\), proving that \(f\) is continuous. If the convergence were only pointwise, continuity of \(f\) need not hold; for example, \(f_n(x)=x^n\) on \([0,1]\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\in[0,1)\) and \(f(1)=1\), which is discontinuous at \(x=1\).

question: In the discussion of uniformly convergent sequences of continuously differentiable functions, how does the uniform convergence of the derivatives \(f_n'\) to a function \(g\) lead to the conclusion that the limit function \(f\) satisfies \(f' = g\)?
answer: Because \(f_n'\) converges uniformly to \(g\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that \(|f_n'(x)-g(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\) and \(n\ge N\). Integrating this inequality from \(a\) to \(x\) and using the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(|f_n(x)-f_n(a)-\int_a^x g(t)\,dt|<\varepsilon(b-a)\). Taking limits as \(n\to\infty\) and noting that \(f_n(a)\to f(a)\) yields \(f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt\). Differentiating both sides shows \(f'(x)=g(x)\) for all \(x\).

question: The lecture notes that the limit of the integrals of a sequence of functions converging pointwise to the constant function \(f(x)=0\) does not equal the integral of the limit. Using the fundamental theorem of calculus, explain how the relationship between differentiation and integration leads to this discrepancy, and state the condition on the convergence that would restore equality.
answer: The fundamental theorem of calculus states that if \(F\) is an antiderivative of a function \(g\), then \(\int_a^b g(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a)\). For a sequence \((f_n)\) converging pointwise to \(f\), the integrals \(\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx\) may fail to converge to \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) because the area under the graphs can remain non‑zero even though the pointwise limit is zero (as in the triangular spikes example). Uniform convergence of \((f_n)\) ensures that the integrals converge to the integral of the limit, because the uniform bound allows the interchange of limit and integration. Thus, equality holds precisely when the convergence is uniform.
